headline: Wreck 3402 in 82 feet: sea bass to 4 pounds, bluefin still working the Mud Hole edges
subhead: The bottom bite never blinked this week while the tuna scattered wide on the temperature breaks — here's where the numbers paid off.
body_markdown:
Wreck 3402, 82 feet of water, about nine miles off the inlet on a heading I've run since before some of you had a boat license. That number's been good to me for twenty years and it didn't let me down this week — sea bass stacked on the up-current side, biggest one going just over four pounds, and enough 14-to-16-inch keepers coming over the rail that we had our limit inside ninety minutes on a Tuesday morning. That's the story of the summer out here: the bottom bite is the one thing you can write down in pen.

Sea bass have been holding tight to structure on Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef too, both running 60 to 80 feet depending where you drop, and the pattern's been the same all month — squid strips on a two-hook rig with 6-ounce bank sinkers, or a Gulp Grub in white/chartreuse on a jighead if the current's light enough to work it vertically. The fish are eating hard on the first hour of a moving tide and shutting down fast once it slacks, so timing your drop to the tide table matters more right now than which wreck you pick. Triple Wrecks, sitting deeper at 105 to 120 feet, has been kicking a few cod mixed in with the sea bass on the bigger pieces — not a fishery you plan a trip around this time of year, but a nice surprise on a bait pickup when you're marking fish stacked tight to the wreckage on the sounder.

The Mud Hole lumps have been the tuna story, though it's been a scattered one. We're a few weeks past the July 3rd trophy closure now, and the recreational slot bluefin bite has settled into the pattern I expect this time of year — fish spread wide across the temperature breaks rather than balled up on one lump. I flagged this exact thing last week, said the tuna bite would hold steady as long as the weather cooperated, and that's exactly what's played out. High pressure's held, the water's stayed clean, and the bluefin keep showing on the same edges — 60 to 90 feet of water on the western lumps, chunking butterfish over a slow-sinking spread once you find bait on the meter. Nothing's been a slam dunk. Three trips out to the lumps this week, we connected on two, and both times it took working the drift, not sitting still, to put the boat over active fish. That's a good ratio for late July, but you still need to find the life — birds working, bait balled tight, maybe a whale surfacing — before you put a bait in the water.

Yellowfin have been the deeper-water target, holding off the canyon edges where that warmer offshore water's been pushing filaments up onto the grounds — we're talking 78 to 80 degree readings out where the Gulf Stream edge meets the shelf, well past what the inshore buoys are reading closer to the beach (NY Bight's been sitting around 71 degrees with a light 4-foot swell out of the south, manageable but enough to make the ride out a little sloppy). Troll-and-chunk spreads have stayed productive out there under this settled weather — green machines and small skirted ballyhoo on the troll, then switching to butterfish chunks once you raise fish or mark bait. That's a longer run than most of my Mud Hole trips, but the consistency's been worth the fuel for guys willing to make the push.

Mahi haven't stacked up yet — not surprised, we're usually two, three weeks out from that pattern setting up hard on the floating structure and weed lines. I've seen a handful of stray fish come up under debris on the way out to the canyon grounds, nothing you'd call a pattern, more a preview of what August usually brings once the pots and pallets start collecting real weed. Worth keeping a spinning rod rigged with a small skirted jig ready on the ride out just in case you cross a piece of structure, but I wouldn't build a trip around it yet.

Bonito are the one I'm watching closest heading into next week. Water's crossed the threshold where they typically show, and the moon's building toward full, which should tighten up the current through Shrewsbury Rocks and the inshore structure where they usually announce themselves first around here. Nothing confirmed in my zone yet, but the ingredients are there — I'd keep a light spinning outfit with a small metal or epoxy jig rigged and ready if you're running past that stretch on the way out to the reef grounds.

Looking ahead: if this high pressure holds through the weekend, I'd expect the sea bass bite to stay the most reliable thing on the schedule, the Mud Hole tuna to keep producing for boats willing to work the drift rather than anchor up and wait, and the canyon yellowfin bite to hold as long as that warm filament stays put on the edge. Watch the moon — full phase midweek should sharpen the current everywhere, which could be the trigger that finally brings the first bonito into the log.
